files.role: writes gazetteer.json and chronology.json for the separate map-system project to consume
files.l1: This file writes two small, human-readable JSON files that a COMPLETELY SEPARATE project (the map system) reads to draw borders and a time slider -- a gazetteer of every place with its coordinates, and a chronology of every dated event, era span, and calendar anchor. These are the whole contract between the two projects: the map repo fetches them at a pinned version, never talks to this server directly.
files.l2: `gazetteer_places(graph) -> Vec<GazetteerPlace>` walks every Place node and folds in its `mentions`-derived attestation verses, producing one row per place (id, canonical name, aliases, lat/lon, provenance, and a `confidence` field that stays `None` for every place today -- kept IN the schema, `#[serde(skip_serializing_if)]`'d away, so a future adapter that captures real confidence data needs no format bump). `chronology_events`/`chronology_spans`/`chronology_anchors` build the matching event/era/anchor rows for `chronology.json`. Both top-level export **struct**s carry an `atlas_version_root: String` field stamped by the caller (`bins/compile_graph.rs`) with the SAME `GraphVersion` `graph.bin` itself reports, so drift between the two files is impossible by construction, not merely disciplined.

files.role: the standalone binary that compiles graph.bin and self-checks it before writing anything
files.l1: This is the one program you actually run to produce the final `graph.bin` file (and the map project's two JSON exports) from all the raw and curated source data. Its most important feature is that it doesn't trust itself: it builds the WHOLE graph TWICE, from two independent code paths, and refuses to write anything to disk unless both builds answer every possible question identically. This is the 'admission' step -- proof, not a promise, that the frozen file matches what a fresh build would produce.
files.l2: `main()` reads `--data-dir`/`--out` command-line arguments, then runs the same `atlas_etl::compile::compile` orchestration the separate ETL binary runs to get an `AtlasData`, reads the raw KJV/xrefs files, and reads every large vendored corpus (brain-fuel multilingual editions, the Book of Concord, Kretzmann's commentary, red-letter data) -- each one HARD-REQUIRED here (unlike `GraphService::build`'s graceful dev-fallback), since a `graph.bin` compiled without them would silently ship an incomplete corpus. It builds the graph TWICE (`graph_a`, `graph_b`) from identical inputs, calls `atlas_graph_types::store::assert_answers_match` between them, THEN also decodes the just-encoded bytes and admits THOSE against the second build too -- proving the actual on-disk bytes round-trip losslessly, not just that the pre-dump graph was internally consistent. Only after both admissions pass does it write `graph.bin`, the red-letter span table, and the two/three map-system export JSON files.
files.l3: The module doc comment frames this file's own reason for existing as a SEPARATE binary rather than a mode flag on the existing ETL tool: the graph-artifact compile step (raw KJV/xrefs + curated eras.toml + already-compiled AtlasData -> one graph artifact) is layered ON TOP of the ETL tool's own curated-TOML+Theographic pipeline, and reads more naturally as its own small tool. The KJV-CASE restoration recompute at line 130 is a deliberate, disclosed SECOND computation of the same restored verse map purely for the startup log AND for feeding the red-letter alignment step (which must run against RESTORED casing, never the raw parse) -- one call serving two purposes, not a third parse of the file. The admission timing itself is measured and printed (`admit_start.elapsed()`), disclosed as 'the expensive check (~3-15s over the full real graph)' that happens HERE, once, at compile time -- never at server startup, which is exactly what keeps the load-time ceiling achievable. The C2/C3 map-system exports and the KRETZ-1 date-mine export are built as a TERMINAL PASS after admission, from the SAME already-admitted `graph_a_indexed`, so `atlas_version_root` in every exported JSON embeds the IDENTICAL `GraphVersion` `graph.bin` itself reports -- drift is impossible by construction, not merely disciplined.
